newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Six foreign aid workers murdered in Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Six foreign aid workers murdered in Chechnya.

text.p: Gunmen killed six foreign aid workers, five of them women, in Russia's breakaway Chechnya early on Tuesday, in the most violent incident of its kind in the turbulent region.

The International Committee of the Red Cross said it was halting its activities in the southern republic of Chechnya after the six were shot dead in their beds in the compound of a recently constructed Red Cross hospital.
President Boris Yeltsin's press secretary said he hoped the killings would not derail the peace process in Chechnya, which Moscow is determined to keep as part of the Russian Federation.
"One has to count on the fact that, despite tragic excesses like these, ...the peace process will nevertheless be maintained and will develop," Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news conference.
Many international aid organisations are active in Chechnya, where tens of thousands of people were killed and many more made homeless in 21 months of fighting which started in late 1994.
The agencies have helped provide medical facilities in a region where power, water and telephone communications are rare.

They have suffered a spate of kidnappings and ransom demands, most of them lasting for only a few days, and at least two aid workers have been killed -- one American and one Finnish. But this is the first incident on this scale.

"We are strongly condemning this attack, which is a serious violation of international humanitarian law. The hospital was clearly marked with Red Cross signs all over it," said Geneva-based Red Cross spokesman Tony Burgener.

"It was an attack on their residence when they were sleeping at four a.m. this morning. It was an assassination." He said the Red Cross workers came from Norway, the Netherlands, Canada, Spain and New Zealand.

The attack took place 17 km (11 miles) from the capital Grozny, in the village of Novye Atagi, where the Norwegian section of the Red Cross built a hospital in just four days and opened it at the end of August.

It had space for over 50 patients and Itar-Tass news agency said it provided work for about 100 local residents, who were paid up to two million roubles ($350) a month -- a fortune for a region where there are few jobs to be had.

Chechen minister Ruslan Kutayev, quoted by Interfax news agency, described the killings as "a deliberate and planned provocation, aimed at disrupting presidential and parliamentary elections on January 27 next year".
Russian forces now have little control over what happens in Chechnya, and power is in the hands of a separatist-led "coalition" government headed by former rebel military commander Aslan Maskhadov.

Both Moscow and Chechnya's separatist leaders are trying to keep the peace settlement on track and rebel leaders have denounced hostage seizures, such as the one last Saturday when rebel commando Salman Raduyev took 21 Russian soldiers captive.
Some Russian officials have warned they could halt the troop withdrawal from Chechnya if there are more kidnappings.
The last of the Kremlin's troops, sent into the region in December 1994 to crush the region's independence bid, are due to withdraw before the regional elections.
The elections are part of the peace deal between Moscow and the separatists, which also defers for five years a final decision on Chechnya's political status.
The rebels still insist on full independence but Moscow hopes to persuade them to stay within the Russian Federation.
There are tens of thousands of gun owners in the region, although violent crime on this scale is rare.
